## Simple explanation

Sampling means selecting some examples from a larger collection or
generating outcomes from a probability distribution. The way examples are
selected affects what conclusions or model behavior they support.

## Technical explanation

A sampling procedure defines how observations are drawn, with or without
replacement and possibly according to unequal probabilities. Statistical
inference depends on the sampling design; machine learning also uses
sampling for train-test splits, mini-batches, negative examples, and
generation.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Sampling affects dataset representativeness, uncertainty estimates,
training dynamics, and evaluation validity. Biased sampling can distort
metrics or model behavior, while random sampling alone does not guarantee
coverage of rare but important cases.

## How it works

Define the target population and selection scheme, draw observations, and
record relevant inclusion probabilities or grouping constraints. For model
evaluation, preserve temporal, user, or entity boundaries when needed to
avoid leakage.

## Practical example

A team can randomly sample production requests for human quality review,
but should also deliberately include rare high-risk categories. Report
results with the sampling method because oversampling certain cases changes
the aggregate estimate unless appropriately weighted.

## Common misconceptions

- A large sample can still be biased if its selection process excludes
  relevant populations.
- Sampling with replacement can produce repeated examples; this is
  intentional in procedures such as bootstrap sampling.
